review_comment: I've put 50 hours into the game so far and have fought every monster at least once and while I am not level 100 yet I have done most of what is available and have been trying out different armor/weapon builds in the end game. The game is definitely fun, although you will likely have to look up guides on the internet to explain certain features and gameplay mechanics. Some skill descriptions are vague and there is no in game description (that I can find) of what certain buffs do so I had to look up external guides for those. This wasn't really a problem for me personally but I can see it being frustrating that the game doesn't provide you all the information you might need to make informed decisions. The addition of focus mode is a significant improvement IMO in terms of combat effectiveness, being able to change the direction of your attacks is huge for this game and has made it much more fun. The game has felt a bit easier than Monster Hunter World, althogh that may just be because I'm more experienced now but I have only failed 1 hunt in my time playing, and that is against what is considered the most difficult monster in game so far, but I've still been enjoying my time and am looking forward to whatever new content they add.

review_comment: If you’re a longtime Monster Hunter fan like me, you probably went into Monster Hunter Wilds with a mix of excitement and skepticism. I was hyped for the seamless open-world approach, but I also worried—would it still feel like Monster Hunter? After spending time with it, I can say Wilds is a bold evolution that mostly sticks the landing, though it’s not without some rough edges. If you’re a newcomer, this is the easiest Monster Hunter to get into. If you’re a veteran, you might find the early game a bit too streamlined, but once you hit the later hunts, that classic Monster Hunter thrill is still very much alive. For me, Wilds is a bold step forward. It doesn’t completely reinvent the series, but it evolves it in ways that make the hunt feel fresh all over again. And honestly? That’s exactly what I wanted.

review_comment: I was extremely excited for this game to come out just as most people were, but this game is the first game where I legitimately have felt scammed by a AAA company. I payed $75 to play a game that was obviously released without proper optimization for PC, and because I love the monster hunter franchise I waited for them to fix it. When they released the announcement for players to check their settings and make adjustments on our end I was upset but still tried it. When the game came out it would crash and I would close the game to look up troubleshooting methods, when they released that first update, the game would crash even faster and sometimes just while I was just trying to lower my settings at the main menu, they put out the high resolution update dlc I downloaded it and now have to cross my fingers and hope to get through the main menu just for it crash before i can even make it to the next monster. All of this just for it to put me over the allowed playtime to get a refund on a game that does not work. Before people start disagreeing and saying that it works fine for them, I'm happy for you but the internet wouldn't be flooded with, videos, subreddits, and review companies all posting potential fixes for this game and it definitely would be at the tipping point of mixed/ negative review on steam.

I certainly hope that Capcom is able to find a way in the weeks ahead to bring computers that meet the minimum requirements and slightly beyond up to a reasonable level of performance. review_comment: Alright so I feel like I can accurately judge at this point. This is one unfinished game broken into three mini games. Yes there are some really cool features, things like traveling up rivers, new units, buildings, and mechanics. But overall this is an unfinished game, and the overarching game isn't for me. As someone who enjoyed civ 5 and 6, as well as Stellaris, this game seem like a speed run to DLC and micro transactions. Instead of a game taking 50+ hours with long drawn out strategies; you can finish a game in 10. My big problem is in Civ 6 you could quickly finish a game on a small map, few players, and with particular strategies, or you could have a giant map with tons of players and have a long drawn out 4X strategy. In Civ 7 this is no option for the later. I feel as if this was intentional in order to sell us DLC and micro transactions. The game stops way too soon. It feels like we regressed in features. Like we no longer can play the way we want, like we can no longer choose our play type. In civ 6 you made decision on how you were going to do things, you made decisions about CO2 use. This in itself was a strategy, especially if you knew your enemies had a ton of coastal cities. Now at the end of an age you get a randomly selected crisis. Instead of having to deal with the consequences of my choices (like CO2 usage or breaking treaties, etc) now things just happen to me. Now I have no incentive to build units until the last game because I will be forced to reset. This games forced balance is forced upon us to attract people who don't like 4X. They are trying to cast a wider net at the expense of core players. This paired with upcoming DLC to finish this unfinished game has me pretty upset. Look at any of the other reviews and they will tell you major features are missing. Its an unfinished money grab. I feel stupid for having pre-ordered and my trust in them is 100% gone.

review_comment: As a longtime CIV fan this game has massive, massive potential. The map is astoundingly beautiful, the new leaders are pretty solid (minus the drawings) and the new civs as well, and things like navigable rivers are so cool for strategic military moves and can make ships relevant for land warfare, However, the game in its current state tips just barely into the category of not enjoyable simply based on how the game triggers certain events and how the AI plays. The ages feature is completely immersion breaking and it's really difficult to stay engaged when the empire you've spent hundreds of turns funding and building is reset at the start of the next age. There are ways around this, for example you save your cities by spending coins in the prior age to ensure thorough building for a higher population, convert to a city, then when it comes time for the next age you're looking at 200-500 coins to turn it back to a city on Turn 1. Granted that's not cheap but if you've built an average economy it's fine-ish. Military you can avoid the reset by focusing on commanders first then units to pack into them. One of these major changes wouldn't be bad but paired with the AI forward settling and rationale behind declaring wars, it makes it nigh on impossible to 1. play anything other than a militaristic game, 2. properly grow towns if placed anywhere near an AI, 3. plan any sort of expansion on any level above Governor. The problem has been discussed at length on Reddit so won't expand here but until the March patch, hold off on the purchase.

The game is completely unpolished. Information that was readily available in previous civ games is missing for seemingly no reason. The game is buggy and multiplayer is STILL unplayable due to bugs and network issues every turn. The gameplay itself is bland and all decision-making or nuance has been removed - in favour of uninteresting "narrative" events and bog-standard linear buildings. The first 2 acts feel utterly pointless. I feel i could spend the first 2 acts of the game sitting on my hands spamming next turn until act 3, where i can then build 3 explorers and a few museums and win the game in sub 20 turns. This game isnt just half-baked, its a shameless cash grab with a gameplay loop that is genuinely boring. Will be playing civ 6 for the forseeable future.

The User interface is the biggest issue with the game, it's Civilization IV interface bad, but manageable. There definitely are many glitches that need work, like how boat won't move when you attack from over two tiles away, they stay in the tile but the icon moves. The city walls sometimes disappear, but are there in spirit. I personally like the new city system, don't have to worry about workers or builders and it goes with the population now which feels more real. The maps are small but beautiful, Civ has never looked this good visually. I recommend it because even though it's very vanilla now, I feel Firaxis has a lot planned for this, so much potential.

review_comment: Tl;dr, The game has serious issues that need to fixed, and while it is has made changes to the standard Civ formula, the changes don't feel like that much of an improvement on previous Civ titles. It does not feel like a step forward, but rather a step sideways, different but not improved. Despite all of this, I do think there seems to be a hard truth in modern game development, in that no game is released completed anymore. Everything is released early access from indie to AAA and is subsequently patched into a completed state. Just because Civ 7 is lacking at launch doesn't mean it will always be lacking, look at Cyberpunk or Helldivers for recent examples. Double despite all of this, if a big name studio like Firaxis is going to release an unfinished, un-beta tested product like this, they have a duty to their consumers to label it as such, and to charge appropriately. $70-$120 is an outrageous price tag for this game, and I really hope the money is going to further development and not to whoever is on the board of 2K

review_comment: Some things I really didn't like was how often I have to repair things - natural disasters damage your buildings, and it's a real pain to have to constantly go into a city and click one at a time to repair. Just wasted clicks, felt like I spent 20% of the time I spent on a campaign doing that. Suggestion for that - give me buildings to handle river flooding and decrease damage chance from other natural disasters. Diplomacy is lacking really any nuance and feels hollow. Influence is even worse and often makes little sense in how I'm gaining or losing it. Wars are a lot of fun, but you often get stuck not being able to make peace due to needing tons of influence to arbitrarily increase your war support to essentially look like you are "winning" - even if have taken most of their cities and decimated their military. Also - post war, you need some kind of forced open borders and a truce period - I often would have units trapped between counties on like - a couple open spaces and the AI would refuse to make an open borders deal/or didn't have influence. Pain to deal with.

review_comment: Civilization VII feels overly scripted, with too much micromanagement required for units. The lack of an auto-explore option for scouts makes early exploration tedious. Era changes are clunky, often making it feel like the game dictates your path rather than allowing for true strategic freedom. I also found the shift in focus from civilizations to individual leaders disappointing. To me, Civilization has always been about the people and the empire they built—not just a single historical figure. On top of that, it feels like the developers are trying to tell players what is fun—pushing an experience they think we should enjoy rather than letting us play our own way. First, there is no Earth map, just some random land and ocean. If you want to play as the United States, you can only choose Benjamin Franklin or Harriet Truman. Franklin was a key Founding Father of the U.S. but was neither a military leader, nor head of state. Although Truman was a great person, who ran the underground railroad, helping countless slaves escape slavery in the south, she was not a military commander, nor head of state. These choices tell you all you need to know about what CIV VII is all about. The focus is in diplomacy and culture. Warfare has so much war weariness that you can't start a war and hope to win unless you have built some huge war machine. In the event that you make it into the Modern Age, you can be crushing the game and then all of your alliances mean nothing and everyone attacks you . War weariness makes your economy fail and your military units are significantly weakened. I could go on, but for me the game was a waste of money. I may give it a few more tries, but I would rather spend my time playing Total War.

review_comment: I suppose I'll start with the positives about this game. It is fun to play. The new ages system is surprisingly well implemented compare to other games that have tried similar mechanics. The game has really high potential. Now, on to the negatives, and there are plenty of them. Let's start with the problem everyone seems to have -- the UI. It's ugly, it's got several bugs, and it's not very intuitive. The tutorial that explains it does a mediocre job and is extremely obnoxious with all of the pop-up boxes all over the place. The Civ 6 tutorial messages were much less intrusive, so that's a nasty downgrade. A LOT of people have issues with it, and I'm no different. Next up is the low number of civs and leaders. Look, I know the game is new, but this is less than both Civ 5 and Civ 6 had at startup. I also get that it will be expanded upon later, but that brings me to my final MAJOR issue with the game -- the monetization. Like far too many new games these days, the game feels like it has had important parts cut off prior to launch for the sole purpose of squeezing the fans for more money, whether that be at launch with the hefty price tag to get everything, or later with the cost of DLC. This has been a problem with most AAA games for years now and it just seems to get more egregious with every passing year. In conclusion, I cannot recommend this game to others in the state it is currently in, nor can I recommend that others pay the current price for it. I am having fun with it and will not be refunding or anything like that, but that is purely because I can see the potential after having played it. That potential needs to be realized before I can advise anyone to buy the game. It should have been whole at launch.

The ages system is wonderful, it carries the game forward in a way that keeps players relatively grouped together and prevents strong starts from dominating the *entire* game. We didn't need to finish the game. This new Ages System keeps strong starts in play, but prevents the continued dominance. That being said, it feels like the game just ends rather suddenly and without much happening at all. Like a fourth, Future Age, is just entirely missing for absolutely no reason at all. Each previous Civ has had a Future age, and now the game ends with biplanes and bombers. Culture Victories just happen when someone finds a 15th artifact. Theres no more need to have player interaction for something as thematic as *Culture*. No trading, no theme-ing, no music, no counterplay outside of vacuuming up artifacts. I can understand merging religion to be a part of culture progression, but by doing so it feels like we've lost an entire gameplay route that synergizes in the ways that Science and Military do. review_comment: Like many others, I've also been a loyal Civ player for 30 years and was very excited for the new iteration. Civ VI has been my favourite, although it took some getting used to compared to the previous ones. Civ VII, though absolutely stunning from a graphics point of view, comes as a pretty big disappointment, unfortunately. I appreciate the fresh take on historical timelines, but part of the fun of playing Civ has always been that you could play the game whichever way you wanted. It allowed us to explore any combination of leader personality and player choices throughout the game. Because Civ VII severely limits these choices, it stunts what could have been a great experience. For example, not being able to cross the ocean until the Exploration Age makes sense historically, I suppose, but it also makes for a very linear, predictable and ultimately boring game. The player has no choice but to wait and then go explore at a prescribed moment. Another example is that during age transitions, players have no influence over certain changes that are invariably going to happen: cities are suddenly no longer cities, peace treaties are made without the player having a say in it, units are automatically upgraded, city recources are redistributed etc. This kind of thing makes me wonder who is in charge of the game I'm playing. It should be me, surely? Overall, it is a visually beautiful game, it is rich in detail and brings some lovely new features (such as overbuilding, new wonders and units, new leader personalities, narrative choices etc.), but to me personally, the gameplay just feels too rigid. After only 6h, I have already lost interest and will most likely return to Civ VI, which I've played for 300+h.

review_comment: Sid Meier's Civilization VII can be surmised by the expression "one step forward, two steps back." While the game in this incarnation has undoubtedly improved in some superficial areas such as the graphics of the map, too many key aspects of what made prior titles in the series fun feel hollow in this iteration. I love the realistic miniature models. Great People have almost been scrapped completely, with some civs having special particular great person units as a unique civ mechanic. Compared to unique great people in 6, this sucks. The UI, while clean, is an overcorrection from VI that lacks even the most basic data one might desire to see. It lacks basic hyperlinks to re-direct you, and as an example, the civlopedia (the in-game reference encyclopedia) is frankly less functional than even Civ 3 or 4's. Civ 6 also did a great job color coding things down to the individual building so as to provide clarity as to what resource x subject was associated with. Civ 7 lacks all of this. Civ 5 had the perfect UI in my opinion, with a detailed yet less is more approach. They doubled down on the sprawling aspect of one's civilization, almost any given hex can have a resource or urban district plopped down on it. For people who disliked the district change in Civ 6, or wonders taking up a whole tile, they've only leaned in further. And no more workers. Cities just instant improve when they grow. Another fundamental problem I have with this game: Content. Or the lack thereof. The tech tree is a good place to begin, and I was shocked at how bare-bones it is in this game versus others in the series. Eurekas are strangely absent, even though the infrastructure to create them is there. What I mean is that there are Eurekas to unlock certain civs in the next age (e.g. if Augustus of Rome wants to transition to Mongolia in the Exploration Era, he needs to either improve 3 Horses or own 3 Siege units). With the whole "History is built in layers" meme they've been leaning into, I expected something like research "alchemy in the age of exploration to get a boost towards chemistry in the modern age", but even that is seemingly too much to ask for. We can count the number of techs in the "Modern Age" with the fingers on our hands: Academics, Aerodynamics, Armor, Combustion, Electricity, Flight, Industrialization, Mass Production, Military Science, Mobilization, Radio, Rocketry, Steam Engine, Urbanization, AND 'FUTURE TECH'. Im sorry but this is garbage and is clearly obsolete by like 1960 historically. What happened to particle physics and stealth tech that even the likes of civ 4 or civ 5 had? As a base-game, with day 1 dlc, this is a joke. Each era I found myself researching future tech an average/upwards of 5 times. I suspect in the future we'll be getting two new ages--prehistory and information era. Thats the only way I can rationalize the lack of options that should otherwise just be there. Religion has been neutered mechanically as well. Basically in antiquity you get a pantheon automatically and in the exploration age everyone founds a religion automatically no great prophet no faith no race/competition just arbitrary global stat boosts and a new types of units for you to start mass producing to counteract AI religious unit fodder. Same with Nukes and WMDs. No tech, you just get them now. Herp de derp. Natural Disasters seem cool until you realize theres like 4 of them and you're only ever going to see the same two on repeat for the whole game. Commanders are nice, and unit stacking in this sense is the happy medium many can get behind. Treasure fleets are a cool idea, but they overlooked basic things, such as treasure fleets being permanently stuck in lakes forever. Game is a buggy mess, with riddled with frustrating bugs/crashes, many of them ruining or corrupting savegames. Where are Scenarios? There aren't even any in this dreaded DLC roadmap, so I assume we aren't getting those anymore. And where are the basic customization options that every other game had? No true earth or earth-like maps avaialable? No changing starting resources to scarce, strategic balance, abundant, etc... Really? Sid Meier's Civilization V has 43 civilizations. Sid Meier's Civilization VI has 50 playable civilizations. Sid Meier's Civilization VII has 29 civilizations. (+2 DAY 1 DLC.) Why should we, as consumers, accept less for more? This is the highest priced Civilization game ever, and yet in terms of a sequel, this title fails every metric it would've liked to have met. Thus far, I see a lot of beloved mechanics scrapped from previous games. I find it utterly distasteful that they will likely be reselling us the same mechanics we already had in increments of $30 dlcs. Im not sold on disconnecting leaders from their civs either. Why not just choose a new leader along with a new civ per age? That makes more sense to me than civilizations like Egypt being locked to antiquity when Egypt was present in all three of the game's ages. There's just something so jarring and confusing about Rome or the Achaemenids declaring war on you and then being shouted at by Harriet Tubman of America. What was Firaxis thinking?!

review_comment: I have loved and played Civilization since 1991. I have really been looking forward to the latest chapter. Honestly, this game is a complete bust. Lots of new ideas in here but it almost like someone shoveled too much content in and forgot to make it a fun game. A few issues. The crisis mechanic: you do everything you can do everything right and the world still melts around you. It reminds me of some of the Total War games I detest the most like Pharoah and Attila. As a player you lose all agency - you are just along for the crummy ride. Part of the joy players take is in building and growing their civilization not having some programmer kick sand in your face. Secondly, you don't have a real cultural transition between ages. It feels like you are given the same map and a new set of rules and a new culture. There is no gradual transition of social and economic dynamics creating a new era as there was in Civ 6 and in history. Finally, the game is a mediocre mess. Wonders stop being wonders and cities sprawl across the map with odd rules governing them. There is a very poor guide and advisors. Honestly, someone should be fired for this game. I will likely be uninstalling it and wishing for my money back unless they patch this thing with a blowtorch.

review_comment: This latest iteration of the legendary 4X franchise is unfortunately unfinished and it's quite frankly astounding that such a commercially and critically successful lynchpin of strategy gaming was pushed out in this barely completed form. The core of Civ VII's game design all seems rock solid, with plenty of novel and interesting features and updates to the classic formula. There is enjoyment to be had for any strategy game fan, and the core "Civ Experience" is intact and improved upon from past iterations, but the game which surrounds this design is woefully unpolished and barely adequate for a $70 price tag. Much has been made about the atrociously unpolished UI, which really is that bad, but this same "cobbled-together" feel applies to almost every interaction-based system in the game. It just feels "off" to play and a distinct lack of feedback from the controls or menu buttons persist throughout every mouse click. I'm sure when this game has received several significant patches, that the core will shine through as a worthy installment in the series, but as of release, it feels as if Firaxis suddenly had their deadlines pushed up by several months to satisfy publisher's quarterly earnings goals. This game is unfinished and laughably rough for a product of its caliber and asking price.

review_comment: But by far my biggest complaint is the lack of player freedom and the pacing of the gameplay. No quick combat/quick movement setting to speed things up here, in fact, 98% of options for creating customized matches have been removed, including the many map variants that were present in previous versions. The game seems intent on forcing the player to do things in a particular order and this impacts your research and civics path, as well as how your cities are developed. No more auto-explore for your scout units, adding a new level of micro-management to the game. Combined with unskippable cutscenes, the match progresses at a glacial pace and feels confined and linear. For me, Civilization games have always been about freedom and experimentation, but this ethos seems to have been abandoned in pursuit of... well I'm not sure, perhaps in pursuit of making the game more accessible to newcomers? I suspect in the end, neither newcomers or returning hardcore Civ players like myself will find much satisfaction in this iteration of the franchise. Luckily, Civ 6 continues to hold up and is still extremely playable in 2025.

review_comment: My final qualms with the game: When you select a leader, the leader looks at you and it's exciting. It's like you, the player, are having a dialogue with this leader, considering all of the possibilities that civilization has to offer. Then you launch the game and you get a two sentence narrated introduction about your leader and your civilization. That's it?! The developers do all this amazing historical research and that's all they give me!? The old Civ V narratives would give me chills. This just felt lazy. And then, when you start playing the game, all of the other leaders don't even look at you! You see your leader talking to the other leader in third person. It completely cuts off that implied dialogue between you, the player, and the other leaders. It weakens the overall connection to the game and the story you are building in your head. It's a subtle change but one that I think massively undercuts the game's potential emotional impact.

review_comment: Let me start by saying THIS GAME WAS 90$ CANADIAN ON RELEASE, a quite frankly ridiculous price for such an unfinished game. The game is poorly configured for the user, with very blocky, awkward UI leading to moments where I couldn't differentiate between certain things on my screen, as well as finding many interaction icons to be unintuitive, leading me to become further distanced from the game. I truly enjoyed Civ 6, and compared to that, this game feels more simplified, to the point of dumbing down the entire gameplay loop so that the player has less to manage. This leads to repetitive gameplay, where you're given less options to make your civilisation's pop-off moments feel powerful, and instead you get a very linear, very simple feeling game. All in all, I do not recommend new or old Civilizations players buy this game until the devs do some serious cleanup.

review_comment: All in all, I'm incredibly disheartened that Firaxis has done their long-standing customers and players this dirty. The longevity of gameplay seems nearly null and void. I'm sure it's great for an introduction to the franchise, but to veteran players such as myself it feels like a blow to the face. There are so many aspects I haven't even touched on, but frankly the ages and legacies are by far the absolute worst part. They are detrimental to the fun I expected to have. I harbour my doubts that Firaxis will undo these horrible aspects, considering they are fundamental parts of the game. I sincerely hope they do, because I have very little interest in playing in this way. It defeats the entire purpose of leading a civilization from an ancient era "on to the stars". I'm legitimately livid and disappointed, and if they don't fix these 2 aspects at the very least, I'm done.

All the new mechanical changes and new features are excellent and add a ton to the game. The only downside I've experienced so far is that the UI is bland. Not non-functional or buggy like others have said, just kinda bland. There are some places where it looks like icons are meant to be, and they're not there yet. It's not enough to make me not love the game. It's incredible. A triumph. If you like Civ, play it. If you've never played Civ before, this is a great entry point. I have played every Civilization game dating back to the original, and this is probably the best one. My previous favorites have been V and II.

All of the artwork from loading screens to science/culture tech looks like a 5 year old scribbled it on a napkin back in 1999. There are no pre-game set-up options. (Like map size, how many opponents, city states, Islands, continents, sea level, temperature, rainfall etc. All there is: New game, pick one of a few leaders, pick one a few civs then the games automatically starts. The game is very simple - as in, it was seemingly rushed to get it to the market where then regular updates will make the game better. THIS GAME SHOULD BE LISTED AS EARLY ACCESS. This game is not worth buying at it's current state. Plus the music is just as horrible as civ 6 maybe worse. only had one repeating native vocalizing chant for an hour and a half. I'm going back to civ6 for a long time I think. What a waste of money.

review_comment: The biggest issue I have with this game is how jarring the age transitions are. I have no issue with the addition of transitions and time periods I think it is a good addition allowing you to start a later game if you want to play a short game. However if I start in antiquity it should not feel like I am starting a whole new game whenever an era changes. It also feels a little unfair that you have worked hard to get ahead of the other civilizations and along comes an age change and everybody pretty much becomes even again. The tech tree should be one continuous tech tree. If you get ahead you get ahead but if you fall behind you shouldn't be rewarded at era change. Also don't take my units away that I worked so hard to build up and give me new units I have no emotional attachment to. I can live with everything else that others have complained about and wait for the updates. The era change overs are the thing that after just 50 hours has me regretting my purchase. If you are a die hard Civ fan that lives for building your empire out of dirt with a single settler stay as far away from this game as possible. I have never felt the need to leave a review on any game in 30 yrs but this pissed me off so bad I felt I had to.

review_comment: civ 7 is, has civ gameplay at its core so it is fun. The problem is they've abandoned the base idea of civ. the idea of taking the civilization you want and basically playing "what if" with them. now, because of the age system, you are forced to play civs you may not want to play. Not only that, but because of this, so much was lost. For example we lost the samurai and everything like that since japan is only a modern era civ. It then gets worse when you play the game. The things that happen when an age transitions don't make any sense as to why they even exist. Age transition ends wars, moves your army and may even delete units, all of your cities (except the capital) revert and have to be repurchased into cities. It really doesn't make the game more "strategic" it just make it more annoying. Another issue is that a lot of thing in the game are lacking in information, or that information is hard to find. Is the game fun? yes. Do i recommend the game? meh. its not a good game. It is fun, but i cant in good faith recommend a civ game that abandoned the core civ idea. The worst part is i don't think its a problem they can fix. The core issue is the age system as a whole. It pains me to say it, but i do not recommend buying this game. Also not having a "one more turn" system is absurd.

The combat is now just pooping out soldiers from generals being troop carriers, no real counter units or even stealth units. The only real positives are river navigation, growing/changing Civs being a fun concept, and the graphics being a massive improvement over 6. The other changes were so mind boggling bad that the game is unplayable compared to 4, 5, or 6. If you want real civ pick up one of those for far cheaper, if you want a quickplay civ revolution game then try this out.

review_comment: It hurts me to write this post, but hopefully it will be for the better. I am a hardcore Civ fan ( +10k hours on Civ 6 that can be validated, and played every sequel since Civ 1 ). Although, I have been very eager to play this new game ( purchased the Founder's pack + taking a full week of PTO just to play it), after 30+ hours the impression is that is just a very expensive early access game, something I would have never expected from 2K or from the Civ franchise. While there are some good factors in the game, as first impression the trading system or the replacement of barbarian encampments with city states, the game lacks a lot of other stuff. It It is very hard to differentiate the urban districts between themselves. Everything looks exactly the same, even the specif quarters need to be zoomed upon to see a difference). But the The one that hit the most for me, I am an epic/marathon player. I like taking my games for several weeks. This game is just not suited for that. I've started with the Roman Empire, being the second in science and I've never actually been able to reach "the wheel" before we've went to the Exploration era...what is up with that ? Colloseum or other stuff were way to head, not even dreaming about them..Where is the scale ? I also get a pop up notification that my relationship with an AI modified ...but that is the whole info...why did it modified, what modified , what made it modified it ??? And I don't even want to start about the crisis eras...that started because an AI destroyed a City State ?? They seem like they are forced to be generated, no matter what, at 75% when the era ends.. why was my Roman empirev affected by that ?? ...and that broke hell all over the continent and it kept it like that for a quarter of an era ??? I will continue to play the game, and I really hope I will have a much better review to put on in the next couple of days, but for the moment, It seems I am gonna regret the 7 days of PTO I took of for this

Then at the turn of the new age your units are automatically upgraded but my siege engines just disappeared. There’s no workers anymore. The cities outside of your capital don’t have production options, only gold purchases. If you’re in war you get a bunch of negative hits towards your civ that keep stacking the longer you’re at war. I read a review that says you can’t dominate the world until the final age. I probably could wipe out the world going into the age right after the antiquity starting age. I invested all my ♥♥♥♥ into military so my legions were just decimating. The city states are weird too. I had one attacking me for some reason, doesn’t say why tho. I started playing Civilization-6 to prepare for Civilization-7. Nothing could prepare me for the boredom or poor graphics found in Civilization-7. Civilization-7 is slow, tedious, and boring. What in the Hell, happened to this product? The game still has glitches, which are probably the only excitement you will find during game play. Sorry folks, as a big fan of this series, this version is worse that Civilization-4, in which the graphics were so bad that I stayed with Civilization-3 until the release of Civilization-5. I get the rational for it, but as others have said, it feels like losing everything you cared about--so, I don't feel compelled to take another turn to make things just a little better. I don't feel invested in the next civilization. The crises feels arbitrary & it feels like the more I tried to build a civ, the more I pay for it when they happen. review_comment: Been a Civ fan since the 90's. Its been my favorite game since then. Was excited for this version. Its garbage. Nothing like what made Civilization great. I tried to give it a go but its just not good. The positive is its visually appealing. Outside of that, there are not a lot of redeeming qualities. You select a "country" but don't expect to play as United States or England, you can be Benjamin Franklin but you have to play as Greece or some other nation. Its dumb. You play the game and then get to a point and everything resets, your units go away, your cities become towns again, basically starting from scratch. Moving the units is a bit glitchy, and you have to repeatedly tell a unit to attack or move before it does it. There's a city limit! HOW CAN YOU CONQUER THE WORLD IF YOUR LIMITED TO 12 -18 CITIES? Its stupid. There is hardly any customization. Your limited to a couple world sizes, a few continent choices and that's it. You cant turn off "space race" which i always did, because I would rather win other ways. Cant do it. Then, once you invested time and win or lose, the game just resets back to main menu. No continuation. You spend all that time, I used to love the option of playing a "few more turns" and finishing what i started. All in all, I wasted money. Posting this so hopefully you don't do the same.

review_comment: In 1994 Sid Meier released a fun little game Sid Meier's colonization. Somehow with Civ 7, the makers succeeded in taking a little bit out of that game and wrongly implemented it in Civ 7. The second age was literally a watered down version of that old colonization game. At the same time destroying what made all the Civ games so great. There is no freedom anymore. An arbitrary city cap for now reason, so you can basically hardly expand by peace. By war then? Nope, same city cap. Is a city wrongly placed on the map, deal with it, because razing a city magically gives all your adversaries military bonuses against you, for the rest of the game, and they stack! So no peaceful expansion, no warlike expansion. This turned the game in a really slow paced watered down Sim City, where you can buy/build some buildings. But only in some of your (artificially reduced number of) cities. This game was so boring, I just quit playing halfway through the second age. What I also missed was this Civ feeling of timelessness, slowly progressing through time. The 3 ages thing destroyed that. Also the huge map, compared to previous civilizations, is pretty small. As a fervent Civ player since the beginning, I was extremely disappointed by Civ 7. I do not recommend this game.

First of all, you should be able to make your units auto explore... it's a no brainer feature and i'm not sure why it wasn't added. Second of all, you should have to option of staying in each age longer than what the game allows... i see no harm in it. If your worried about staying in a certain age giving you an advantage; make it a feature you can turn on and off in the advanced settings. With that being said... WHERE IS MY ONE MORE TURN option!! Why can I not play more turns on a game that is finished... also a no brainer feature. The last thing I can think of is the map selection, why can I not play on an earth like map and why can I not make the map humungous... the largest it goes is standard. I just feel like for civ to be hard it requires a lot more space than whats offered on the standard map. Last thing, people have been saying the game feels like its in beta... it really doesnt. It just needs a couple of finishing touches. I have confidence these issues will be addressed. Games arent perfect and you can clearly tell a lot of care was put into creating this game. The PC version seems better, and made it through to the first age change without crashing. It's still a bit aggravating though. Units don't do what you want them to do, and I can not figure out how in the world I'm supposed to get merchants to make a trade route? Says I have available routes, but nothing happens. I expected bugs, I purchased Cyberpunk when it launched on PC, other than some graphics issues, I found that game to be very playable, this one, not so much. I know I spent a great deal of money to be BETA tester, but I've played this game since the beginning. I'm not an expert, and always find things out the hard way at times, but this game lacks any intuitive inputs and does not do what you expect. I am not impressed at all. Civ6 was nowhere near this messy and I play on both platforms, the console version is nowhere as good as the PC, but it at least worked. Very sad that the developers have done what so many others have done and put out a game that is not ready.

review_comment: I have given Civ 7 three weeks of solid play and my overwhelming opinion of the game is negative. I think the four main problems with the game are 1) There are too few ages. Simplifying this aspect of the game completely removed so many layers. 2) The oversimplification of the game mechanics removes synergy and complexity. In previous versions of the game all of the different aspects of the game would affect each other ensuring that no two games were alike. This version lacks the creativity of the earlier versions and just comes out flat. Rome Total War I has more layers. 3) Being that I often like to play the conqueror the fact that most of the military units disappear when the age changes is a deal killer. 4) All of these factors, plus several dozen smaller changes, that just look like the designers were trying to cut corners, culminate in one result - Civ 7 is not fun.

As others have noted, the eras are not a good feature. Forced progression to the next era without completing the tech tree doesn't make a lot of sense. Civilizations seceding each other that don't really have a directly link doesn't make a lot of sense. Ben Franklin, leader of the Romans? And the worst part, it seems like every version is geared more and more against colonialism. It's an empire building game! Colonialism is the point!! I'm ok with having different tools like culture in addition to military conquest, but they are more and more punishing for trying to build a large empire to the point now that you actually have very small limits on the number of cities. Which aren't even cities to start. Who the heck decided that initial towns can't do anything on their own or produce things on their own and you have to just spend money to make stuff happen? Besides that, the game is buggy. Has problems saving games locally. Crashes for me between era's. I prepurchased the deluxe edition to play a little early. Very big regret. Wish I could have my money back.

review_comment: After giving the game and it's new features a chance I did have fun but until the developers fix the many issues present, this installment of Civ will never be as popular or re playable. Beyond the horrible UI, the game and civilopedia don't explain new features well... or at all. Want to look up radioactive fallout to see how to get rid of it since there aren't workers anymore? Good luck. Maybe it dissipates after a few turns? Not sure, the eras are too short to really find out and the game forcibly ends after a victory condition! Think you leveled up your leader to get some of those bonuses that are frustratingly locked behind hundreds of hours worth of gameplay? Guess again! The game doesn't accurately trigger most of the challenge criteria, how many full games do I have to play before it registers that I've completed the antiquity era even once! The settlement cap is a joke, you have to put up with the other Civs spamming cities near you until you can take them then have to decide whether to keep them against your limited cap or get permanent war support against you?! I'm not sure that feature even works because the cities take forever to raze vs how short the eras are. Choose to go over that settlement cap and start incurring unhappiness in your cities, what are the consequences? Do they rebel, do they not grow, do they reduce yields? Other than a one and done notice that your people are unhappy and that it's bad... I have no idea! Not to mention the city screen doesn't itemize so you learn how to fix happiness issues. Why can't I pick which building to overbuild, the game chooses for me? Why?! Why can't I deconstruct buildings because there's so many and you can't realistically city plan well based of adjacency bonuses over multiple eras. No workers..? This one is controversial, I get that workers were removed to cut down on micromanagement fatigue but then they also removed auto explore... so you are forced to micromanage that instead. The worker micromanagement fatigue was real by the end game BUT that's always how I felt that I excelled and won against the odds playing on high difficulties because I was able to extremely efficiently manage and optimize my Civ vs the average player or computer. This game tried to level the playing field for people who haven't played or casually play and don't deep dive into how the game works in order to be good. I read somewhere that the eras being split was meant to avoid the player or computers from getting too far ahead or It very much feels like cheap rubber band mechanics from early racing games where no matter how well you played the computers were rubber banded at 500 mph to catch back up with you... and people hated that 2-3 decades ago, why would they reintroduce such a horrible concept? The game is fun to play for short periods of time but the frustration will keep me from playing like I played the other games. It feels like a Civ imitation almost, this release significantly lowered my opinion of the developer's ability to either create a true Civilization main entry or realize that their work wasn't nearly ready for launch. I'll check back in a few months or a year to see if they've decided to release a real $140 quality product then.

This is also not a 4X game, as the stupid settlement cap removes the incentive to expand, I appreciate it was in CIV5 but was glad when it vanished in CIV6. The game play is shoddy and disjointed, the City and Town premise for me doesn't work. While the game may look pretty, it also hides a lot of information, and is difficult to see some critical data. At the moment this game feels more like an early access game rather than a supposedly ready to go. There is so much missing around Religion, Diplomacy as well as the final victories it almost not worth the effort to play, I will give the developers a chance to improve, but at the moment CIV 6 is 10X the game of its successor.

review_comment: The ages concept is a bold change to the usual Civ formula, and whilst it could be finessed it works very well on the whole. It gives intermediate goals, rather than a long slog to the end,. It also makes it easier for new cities to catch up with established ones, because a modern settlement doesn't need to build all the antiquity and exploration era buildings, which are being overbuilt in your old cities anyway. Overall, the ages system simultaneously makes your buildings and techs more immediately impactful, whilst still giving the ability for civilisations to catch up between ages.

review_comment: Windows 10 & 11 has something called a RADAR_PRE_LEAK service which tries to detect a potential memory leak in an application and deal with it before it becomes a bigger problem. After uninstalling my video drivers and attempting other fixes, I began surfing other discussion boards and noticed a considerable number of submission mentioning Steam specifically. So I tried a simple test; I put Steam into offline mode. Low and behold; the issue went away. Back in Online mode; it came back. The issue is not with the game, it is with Steam during Online mode doing something that RADAR_PRE_LEAK doesn't like. If you experience this problem and see the Windows dialog box that "Sid Meier's Civilization VII (DX12) is not responding... try putting Steam in Offline mode.

review_comment: I'm a huge Civ fan and I have played all the previous versions, I was so excited to play this game with my husband using hot seat. It's the only game we like to play together. I spent $139, only to find out that there is no hot seat! We are so disappointed. The disappointment continued when I kept playing alone. The graphics are stunning, but it feels like this is the only improvement to the game. There's not enough tutorial or UI tips to explain how this new game works. The abrupt end to the ages is so frustrating and then the abrupt end to the game is even more frustrating. My game ended in the 1800's! This makes no sense at all. It takes an insane amount of turns to get tech, so you can only get about 2 tech upgrades per age which is very limiting. The game moves so fast at standard speed, you don't have any time to do things properly. All of the ageless buildings are ancient, so you can't build anything cool in the modern era. Towns disappear for no reason at all. Poof they are gone. All the money and time you spent on them is wasted. I later discovered you have to spend money to make them a City. Again, a tip from the tutorial would have been handy. I don't want to spend hours reading the help file to learn how to play a game that I've been playing all my life. If you are going to change a game so drastically then please provide a better tutorial, so people understand what is going on. I'm really regretting buying this game and I'll be going back to playing Civ 6. The game is beautiful, but not fun anymore.

review_comment: Playing Civ games since Civ 2. I usually don't do reviews but with this pricing compared to the recieved product I feel obligated to write this. On first impression it feels oversimplified. No advanced options on game creation, no huge map to get lost in, no pangea, no map tweaking. And ok, that can be added but for 130 euros... Next on the list is a thing that I don't know if it can be fixed: Age transitions---immersion breaking, makes me wanna instant alt+f4 the game. I finally lose myself in the game and then age changes, I lose my cities they become towns again, for some reason I need to change civilizations, everything I've been working on up until that point becomes meaningless. And why this any leader any civ mixing criss crossing??? Why??? And then again mixing during the game? Why? Even if it that wasn't confusing as is. Part that I don't like about it is that it loses the educational part of civ. Yes, Civ games used to be medidative (no need for immerssion breaking, let me be lost in my sp game on huge map for tens of hours) and Civ games used to be educational we learned bits of historical knowledge while discovering technologies, wonders, world wonders etc. Leaders were connected to their civs and we learned about them and why are they important for country they represent. Navigable rivers are great, the reworked diplomacy feels much more thorough than in 6, the new resource system is more engaging than before, the map (though small) has great terrain details, the new independent power system is less irritating than barbarians were, and the three-age system seems cool. I think lots of people are over-eager to criticise the game (seeing the amount of negative reviews scared me at first), but after playing more than many of these reviewers, I think they are mostly basing their opinions on the (admittedly not great) UI. Then the age ended because I got too much science or culture or something and when we entered the next age my army was gone and everyone was at peace. Overall the game shows great potential but it's just so frustrating the way it forces you along, including booting you out at the end of the game. What ever happened to "Just one more turn..." Why can't I keep going and take over the world after getting some other win condition? It's so damn disappointing. In previous Civ games I could always turn off all the win conditions except domination to give myself time to build a powerhouse and steamroll the other civs. Now it's like I'm just plugging away building and expanding and then the game suddenly says, "OK, you won, now get out." Do not even get me started on the UI. it is a colossal mess of chaos! Nothing is clear to the eye and you have and must truly decipher the screen to figure out what is what. Also, no matter what your mouse DPI one experiences consistent and frequent difficulty in item selection. Game play is rather limited and condensed and now broken down into three different mini-game ages, in which you must change the leader you are playing with each time. The game is just incredibly designed badly and can only piss off any true Civilization fan. I requested a refund for my purchase of the game and the upgrades I also purchased with the game expecting good results and lots of hours of fun only to be grossly let down. But the ultimate reason I demanded a refund is that the game is no longer playable due to a Fraxis loading crash error. i did manage to give this game some 170 plus hours of game play trying to decipher its mechanics and too gain a will to play and enjoy and like the game. Game has been running smooth with only minor audio glitches and the occasional unit ghost image on a hex. Nothing that has caused me to stop playing. I have largely enjoyed most of the changes they made to the game. The ability to group units with commanders is huge to reducing micro-managing during larger conflicts. The building/upgrading system took me a minute to understand but its simple enough to grasp. The biggest change for me was the dynamic civilizations system or whatever its called that forces you to change civs every age. In the end, i came to love it. review_comment: The price is too high, simple as that. Ben Franklin is B tier so long as he can stack influence which is his whole thing. He does get science bonuses, but you won't feel them until the late game, making his early game rather meh. Isabella is sufficiently broken that she's genuinely stupid to go against. I usually exclude her in games I play because she's stupidly broken. She gets double bonuses on cities with natural wonders, and she gets treasure ships for having them. It's stupid. She's double S tier. Why won't they fix her? review_comment: Yes, the UI is bad. A completed game with a pre-alpha UI. Yes, they left out a couple of integral features like teams, a variety of map types, and map sizes. HOWEVER, they did an amazing job with gameplay and the changes to CIV's core mechanics. In my opinion, Civ 5 (in its finalized state) was a masterpiece for the time. It lacked several things, namely a variety of gameplay strategies to progress towards victory other than blitzing science first above all else. Civ 6 fixed that issue and introduced a variety of other, more dynamic strategies. However, Civ 6 screwed a lot of that up and made several mistakes in the implementation and depth of those systems. Civ 7 LEARNED from those mistakes and it finally feels like they've made the game they had intended all along. Your choices matter. They carry depth and have implications hundreds of turns down the line. There is an immense amount of variability and viability of strategies to come out on top, and I cannot wait to explore more of them. Yes, it has its issues. And it's sad that the state of gaming today is releasing unpolished, arguably unfinished games. But as far down as that list goes? Civ 7 is FAR from the bottom. Where I'd wait a year or two for most triple A games, or several years for titles like No Man's Sky to come around, I couldn't be more excited to see the state of the game a month from now, after the first major update releases with UI changes amongst everything else. Because the issues I have are minor in the grand scheme of things.

review_comment: While the game might look pretty, there is a lot they removed that made that made the Civ games worth playing. The same is true about the things they changed or added. They removed the ability to play longer games. I always enjoyed using domination as the victory condition since it allowed me to play for hours on a single map. Now, you can't set victory conditions and the game feels very short, even with the long ages setting. There is only three eras to go through, again, this is too short. The new age system where you select a different civilization at the end of each era is neat, but I'd much prefer not being forced to move forward with everyone else once each era is over. Each of the three eras has a limited number of turns before the game arbitrarily forces you into the next stage, there is no way to turn it off. Civilization V is my ideal game from the series. Also, out of all the ships from the "modern" era for Japan, you decided to use the Mikasa and not the Yamato. What is wrong with you? All in all, the game does not feel like a Civ game. It's a completely different game, and should have been a spin off and not considered a sequel.

review_comment: I'm not a game developer or any related job title. I don't know the process that goes into making a game like this. But it seems like this game was released, not just a bit unpolished, but entirely unfinished. There are core mechanics that don't work as intended or described; a wildly perplexing UI downgrade from the previous installment; plenty of bugs that, frankly, I don't know how the dev team didn't see during development, from disappearing UI elements, to events for one leader that only pop up if you reload a save, to very reproducible disappearing yields and resource icons during the FIRST TURN OF THE GAME; and a complete lack of a useful in-game guide to the game. If the UI was complete, a guide wouldn't be necessary. But there are so many features that you can only really figure out after spending dozens of hours playing this game. And since some mechanics don't work, you're never even sure if what you learn will change in the near future as the devs process bug reports and feedback. Don't get me wrong, it's fun so far. But I wouldn't buy this game for at least another year.

review_comment: And yet, despite these caveats, I do think Civ 7 is a good and fun game. If it were not called "Civilization," I suspect it would have a much smaller customer base but would also be heralded as a brilliant little 4X game. Ironically, the game is trying to appeal to everybody in some ways, and to very specific types of players in others, and the expectations the marketing wing of 2K set are simply not in line with the game design. But if you do like Civ-as-board-game, and you don't mind zany leader/civ combos, there's a lot to like here, especially once they do their obligatory bug fixing and UI polishing. For my part, I already enjoy Civ 7 much more than I did 6 or 5 (though 4, particularly the Fall from Heaven mod, remains my favorite). Is it a perfect game, no. Should you buy it if you are a casual Civ fan, probably no. But if Civ is your favorite PC series of all time and you prefer what came before 6 then you will probably like this one. I find myself thinking about it constantly when not playing and it really does give you that one more turn feeling. I'm already having more fun than I ever had with 6.

Beyond that, it's really not bad. It has a lot of interesting things going on. Some of the other reviews was worrying me that it was going to be vastly different from the other games in series, but that's not really the case. It is quite different than any of the other ones I played, but it it's still quite a bit of fun with some interesting new features. Definitely a change to get used to compared to the other ones in the series, but it's worth a shot. I would recommend giving it some time because there's a layer of polish missing that makes the game a little disappointing as of now.

As a dedicated fan, I purchased the Founder's Edition the moment pre-orders went live, only to be met with a product that feels unfinished and poorly optimized. The UI is a glaring mess, failing to deliver even basic functionality, let alone a visually pleasing experience. The scaling options are a disaster—enabling them results in a cluttered, unreadable interface, while disabling them makes the UI proportions even worse. The font choices and readability are equally subpar. This is not the quality I expected from a franchise I hold in such high regard. You owe your loyal players better than this.

review_comment: Despite the ages being more disconnected than what I like, there is a ton more that contributes to me recommending Civ 7. Each age is very unique, presenting its own challenges and stories. The uniqueness and freshness to each age made me want to play even more, and discover new ages that may be in the works. Being able to level up leaders over time, and unlock specific abilities makes the game cohesive and encouraging from one campaign to the next. The combat in Civ 7 is fresh and innovative. The overal game is gorgeous (minus the leaders being reminiscent of an early 2000s poorly rendered art style). There are also so many narratives that drive the story forward. What makes me recommend this the most is simply just the ideas and foundation of Civ 7. I understand frustrations on DLC and price. Yet in my opinion, at launch the game does feel mostly complete. DLC is going to ensure that these ideas stay fresh and innovative over the entire life of Civ 7. Yes, there is work to be done (primarily in UI)--- but developers have already confirmed player wants/needs are heard, considered, and acted upon. Once this work is done, Civ 7 will easily stand the test of time.

With it not helping explain basic game concepts such whats happening to my yields during overbuilding or reverting back to a one city state after transitioning from eras. This is two among a number of quality of life issues or whatever you want to call them. The UI needs help as well but I believe once the game is finished it will be much better. I do like the introduction of leveling up player levels and having character levels for individual characters. Just would've liked to know they were there before I started a run. The era system, civ system, leader system and many new changes are very cool and I believe there is so much here to work with, but the transitions need a massive amount of work. Where it sits, at its absurd price mark, the game is not near deep enough. Will it get there? I hope so. review_comment: Update: This is a critical review, yet I would recommend it. I have purchased the version also for console and I am happy about the crossover capabilities and the fact that I can play it there / you need to buy the game two times though. Anyway as I said, this version is not one for hardcore PC fans. But it does provide some kind of enjoyment. Like I mentioned in my original text which follows, they could still have left some key binds open. Also, and this is something I must persist on, allow us to END turns despite open moves etc. Original and critical review, which still holds to the points I made: I do not know how they can make a perfectly fine recipe for success fail so miserably. I have played and own all cid meiers civs. This one is on par with III/IV as to how bad a game can become. I am glad that the AI doesnt bother me that much with their endless bla bla bla. But the whole game is in strip it down / dumb it down mode. I do not mind the leaner aspect of the game, but some stuff like not being able to queue science tree, or that i have to click hundred times to make an trade icon move to a city or trade routes that aren't working properly, or the fact that you still cant attack with your army for some odd reason, and without explanation - everything is grayed out, here would be a welcome time for some tips in-game. The fact that they made a complete mockery of world history, removed major leaders like some Roman emperors and Greek leaders is beyond me, but I could give the company some slack if they at least tried. The fact that the images are somewhat better means nothing nowadays, its expected. The legacy stuff and like I said the leaner policies is also good. Crisis scenarios with random people starving or being ill and you having to get less gold from an altar is far fetched logic, but ok. So all-in-all ill try to complete one scenario but I doubt if Ill ever play this again. I would advise ppl not to spend so much cash on this game till maybe after feedback from the community they patch and revamp major problems. Now more hours in, started war, ofcourse. And its been 30 years in the making people and they still can't fix the attack targetting problem of units! its impossible, that you have to click 200 times from your unit to another to make the attack happen, sometimes having to rotate camera, zoom in, zoom out. NO this does not make the game feel "close to home" it makes it feel u threw away cash for some minor visual changes and leaner edition. And lastly and most importantly, I get it, we all want Civ to flourish and expand to mobile and TV / console, but seriously not one Keybind? At least give back the option to END TURN no matter how many things need to be done. The world keeps spinning, time keeps flowing even when you are just deciding to NOT build something or move a piece or change policy. Please be a bit more realistic. Also... there is no graph I have noticed about how you are doing compared to others, no score towards victories or if there is I havent seen it. You can only see the per round yields of the other players. On the plus side the general feel of the game flow when ignoring the above stuff that could be to be honest easily patched, is smoother. But it lacks the depth we know Civ has. I might make a general pros/cons list for this review to be more easily readible. Im not one to spend time to write reviews, but Civ is something I believe everyone should have played at some point and if one expan makes it less than what it was/should be, it might be a blow to the legacy. As aforementioned, the mobile/console expansion could be dealth with a tad better, the controllers do have some buttons and mobile devices also allow numerous interactions.

review_comment: I did not recommend this game initially due to a glitch that made marathon speed unplayable, specifically warning other marathon players like myself to be aware of the issue if they decided to buy the game. The glitch caused the ages to progress too quickly, at the same rate as a standard speed game, whilst having all of the research and production progress at the rate of a marathon speed game, essentially making it impossible to progress in any significant way. I had only managed to complete three exploration technologies by the end of the exploration era in my first playthrough, and completing a legacy path was an impossibility. With the recent patch, the issue has been fixed, and I no longer have any major gripes with the game. It is only fair that I update my review to reflect this change as a result.

review_comment: Civilization VII introduces significant changes compared to its predecessors, offering enjoyable combat mechanics, city-building, and overall gameplay. However, the game’s age system feels too drastic, often disrupting progress rather than fostering a natural sense of advancement. The age transitions frequently reset key aspects of the game, including the economy, trade routes, and sometimes even adjacency bonuses, which can throw off carefully planned strategies. In some cases, the transition may even result in the deletion of army units, further hampering progress. Because each age feels so distinct, I often found myself fixing my economy and production rather than progressing smoothly through history. A more balanced approach—where only dark ages impose severe penalties—would help maintain a sense of continuity. Additionally, some civilizations feel unbalanced. For example, the Normans’ basic soldiers are mere swordsmen, while the Spanish enter the Middle Ages equipped with muskets, creating an unfair advantage. Hopefully, future updates will address these issues, refining both the age transitions and civilization balancing for a smoother and more strategic game play experience. Overall the game is enjoyable and music is amazing I hope the age transitions are improved.

review_comment: I've played the game for 85 hours so far. Games are far shorter than any other version I have played. I've had games of Civ 6 that have lasted more than 20 hours. I just won my latest for this version in less than 6 hours of total play and can't even really tell you why I did (and I have no idea why I won the previous 3 times, either). The game just suddenly says "Victory!" The end. The video that gets played doesn't have words to explain my victory (maybe Gwendolyn Christie was too expensive and that's why she narrates less than previous versions). They make a big deal about the pathways to victory. I was no where near winning any of the times I won. In fact, the AI had met the conditions to win, fulfilling their pathway to victory long before the game suddenly ends. I'm obviously incorrect about how to win, but I only have this misconception because the game guide was buggy AF. The first 4 times that I played (after it stopped quitting every few seconds), I got different guide screens each time and I'm not talking about it being because I was doing different things. I'm talking about general knowledge. Like how to work a commander or how treasure fleets work. Every time I played, the guide explained something different (the first time I played, it gave me a lot about settlers, but never told me another thing about any other civilian pieces). By the time it finally got around to giving me more knowledge, I had already looked it up online out of frustration, until I finally got annoyed with the guide enough to turn it off and just resort to YouTube. Some of my biggest gripes are going to be fixed, like the lack of automation. I do not want to spend half the game moving my scouts or ships around to explore. And the maps are boring AF. I've gotten the same exact map with almost no variation 3 times now (tiny islands were vaguely different). My other biggest gripes are with the game itself. I've played Humankind. This is Humankind with better graphics. I did not like Humankind. It was boring. The vast majority of that game and this game are busy work. Earliest part: explore and get settlements faster than the AI while surviving hostile tribes. Middle part: expand your settlements, add a few more, finish some districts in your settlements and cities. End part: everyone jumps to war with you for no reason so you abandon your building mindset to crush the AI, which is easy because you're making 2k a turn in gold, so you just keep buying planes and tanks. And then you randomly win. At least with Civ 6 there were fun ways to go after the AI like stealing cities because your civilization has the best riz, or the secret society stuff. Religion doesn't really matter. I stopped making missionaries because it's too easy to convert settlements and you barely get a benefit from it. I've obliterated multiple other civilizations in one game and not advanced in the military victory path. In the first 6 games that I played, I had no idea how to get artifacts because, yet again, the guide never told me and the help section is useless. A lot of things in the game are not intuitive, like the artifact thing, and there's no info in the game on how to make them work, so it's just frustrating trial and error or you just give up because you can do other things to win (or nothing at all because who knows). I cannot explain to you how often the game just won't let me buy a district for a settlement with zero explanation. I have no idea if that's a bug or if there's a reason. The districts are just not on the menu, not even the hidden one, for that place. And finally, though I still have a lot more to complain about, when you move from one age to the next, things reset. Did you pay to make that settlement a city? Poof, gone. Your giant military that you were just destroying the AI with? All gone if they weren't attached to commanders. Money, influence, science? Poof. Poof. Poof. I'm going to go back to playing 6 until they iron out a few of the issues. Then I guess I'll come back since I payed a lot for this stupid game.

review_comment: Despite its promising visuals, Civilization VII feels like a step backward for the series. As a veteran with 2000+ hours in Civ V and VI and experience since Civ II, the biggest issues are the awkward UI and poor information display. While cities look great, it's hard to tell what you've built, and the map lacks readability. The new commander system adds interesting tactical depth, but removing unit skill levels makes individual combat feel meaningless and less fun. The gutting of resource strategy mechanics removes another layer of meaningful decision-making that made previous games engaging. Limiting settlers through the happiness system feels like artificial restriction rather than good game design, and the removal of builders reduces player agency. Basic features like automated exploration are mysteriously absent, making the game more tedious than fun. Even after several hours, it's still unclear how many units you can support or why AI civs suddenly plant cities between your territories. Between the simplified resource system and other streamlined mechanics, it's hard to find the engaging strategic elements that made previous titles so addictive. While the game might improve with patches, this feels like more than a few balance tweaks away from greatness. The simplified systems and clunky interface suggest a troubling shift toward console gaming conventions - a cardinal sin for a franchise that helped define PC strategy gaming. The Founder's Edition currently feels like a waste if money.

review_comment: I have thousands of hours into the history of the Civ franchise and love it. I purchased the founders pack hoping that all the hype was worth and new Civ game. Civ 7 is a very different from what Civ players love and enjoy about the game. This rendition is broken into 3 mini games (ages) that loosely hold continuity together. The 3 ages have way to much history crammed into a sub age, but is managable. You need to play in marathon to enjoy all of it. There are some new features introduce that are a good addition to the game but the split of three ages breaks the immersion of being a civilization playable through time. You have to choose a different culture each age. There are many missing features that need to be put back into the game to make it more playable. They took out auto-explore, unit UI control, limited tech trees. A very awkward town to city sub system that you have to invest heavily into to gain any resources or usability from expanding from more than your one city. Then you have all of that ripped away at the abrupt end of an age. At that transition you lose cities, (turn back into towns) which you have to buy and then build up again to be useful. All but a few units are destroyed and those few are put in there place at that age level. You have to start over in the new age and re-chose how you are going to play in the segmented mini games. Many of the new features seem to have been copied from Humankind in how the civics and policies come into play and many more added in to pop up at certain tech levels. The map sizes are way to small to play any decent game, tiny, small, and standard. Standard is a very cramped map. The map seeds usually place most of the AI Civs within a city area away from you. Not to mention all of the hostile (barbarian) city states which you have to dump tons of resources into just for a hope that they wont attack you constantly. The city states are able to pump out units every turn and wage war on you as the AI Civs do the same. Attempting to survive the onslaught of the AI gang-banging you while trying to complete quests inside of each mini game is a miracle. Even though if by some chance you might be crushing the globe under your foot, to then lose at the abrupt end of the age if you haven't completed enough quests. It is a steep learning curve and have to micro mange every detail to achieve success. I do recommend playing marathon mode with all tutorials on for the first play through.

review_comment: Boring boring boring. Way too similar to Civ 6 but without the complexity and absorption. Was hoping for Civ specialisation in play style such you get in Warhammer III, with different civs playing out their own end goals differently to each other, but there is not enough imagination in Civ 7 to make it worth the completely exorbitant price. At times boring, at times opaque, and some baffling choices such as it didn't seem possible to play a civ such as Charlemagne actually as the Frankish. What? Game mechanics such as climate, religion and natural disasters have all been hollowed out and simplified so as to be nothing short of annoying, with nothing you can do about them except repair stuff. The three historical segments of the game allow more time and fun in the Ancient times than previous games allowed, but as the ages progress the choices become more and more limited and the 'modern' stage is a joke. The game is fatally married to scientific progress so if you haven't got a civ with good science, you fall behind and lose simply by dint of time running out. They have dispensed with the modern armour category and you can't progress your armour beyond a Sherman tank. Still the same old Science, Culture, Military or Economic win goals and, surprise surprise, you have to build a rocket to the moon again. Lazy game design and poorly executed ideas. Nothing new. Actually just slightly north of bad.

The game is so feature-rich but explanation-poor that you can't do much else but fumble your way through it. And as soon as you start to feel like you've got a handle on things, the game completely disrupts your gameflow and you find yourself asking "wait, why are all my cities unhappy?" or "how am I generating *negative* science*?" or "why does my gold mine keeping getting destroyed?" or "Hey why did my Commander just die and where did all the units in his stack go?" That fact that 2K pushed for DLC to be ready at launch when the base game is in this state adds insult to injury in my opinion. I hope the game will get better, but if you're considering buying it, just save your money and time and wait for the game to be fixed.
